questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Ceiling?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kisame” = ceiling. Clipped from Spanish zaquizamí, which came from Arabic for “roof in the sky” (per Wiktionary). Memory hook: the ceiling is the sky of the room; pair it with sahig (floor).

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Floorboards is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Dotal” = floorboards. Origin not confirmed and not obviously Spanish. Memory hook: dotal ~ “dots”: the rows of nail dots across a floor of boards.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Mezzanine?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Entresuelo” = mezzanine. Origin: Spanish entre “between” + suelo “floor”: the floor between floors.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Baseboard?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Rodapis” = baseboard. Origin: Spanish rodapié “baseboard”, from pie “foot”: the strip at the foot of the wall.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Cement tiles?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Baldosa” = cement tiles. Origin: Spanish baldosa “floor tile”.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Flooring?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Suelo” = flooring. Origin: Spanish suelo “floor, ground”, from Latin solum.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Plank board?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Senepa” = plank board. Origin: Spanish cenefa “trim, border”. Senepa covers any trim board. The same term is also used for: fascia board, riser, skirt.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Wainscoting tiles?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Asolehos / Asolejo” = wainscoting tiles. Origin: Spanish azulejo “glazed tile”, from Arabic az-zulayj. Asolejo sounds like azulejo.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Wood grain is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Haspe” = wood grain. Likely from Spanish jaspe “jasper”; jaspeado means streaked or veined, like wood grain.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Hall is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Caida” = hall. Borrowed from Spanish caída “fall, drop”. In the traditional bahay na bato it typically names the hall at the head of the stairs.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Wood plank?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tabla” = wood plank. Origin: Spanish tabla “board, plank”.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Floor?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to External siding?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tabike” = external siding. Origin: Spanish tabique “partition, thin wall”. External siding is the thin boarded wall.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Kiln dried wood is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Tuyong Kahoy” = kiln dried wood. Origin: Tagalog tuyo “dry” + kahoy “wood”. Literally dry wood.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Skirt is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Senepa” = skirt. Origin: Spanish cenefa “trim, border”. A skirt is the trim board at the lower edge. The same term is also used for: fascia board, plank board, riser.
